title: Tenali Raman and the Well on the Riverbed

full_text:
A spiteful and jealous neighbor named Lingaiah sought to ruin an honest vegetable farmer named Somu.
Somu owned a piece of fertile land bordering the dry summer riverbed of the Tungabhadra. During the dry season, Somu dug a shallow sand well in the dry riverbed to water his gourds.
Lingaiah brought a lawsuit before King Krishnadevaraya:
'Maharaj! The riverbed belongs to the crown! Somu has dug a well on imperial river territory!
I demand that Somu be ordered to remove his well immediately and take it away from the riverbed, or be imprisoned!'

The King, in a hasty mood, accepted the literal argument and ordered:
'Somu, within twenty-four hours, remove thy well from the riverbed!'

Poor Somu came weeping to Tenali Raman:
'How can I remove a well? A well is a hole in the ground! If I dig it up, it is only dirt!'

Tenali smiled: 'Fear not, Somu. Tomorrow morning, Lingaiah shall help thee remove it.'

The next morning, Tenali Raman, Somu, and twenty village laborers arrived at the dry riverbed with spades, ropes, and baskets.
King Krishnadevaraya and Lingaiah arrived to inspect the removal.

Tenali bowed to Lingaiah:
'Master Lingaiah, we are ready to remove the well!
We have brought spades and bullocks to haul the well away to Somu’s private field.
However, according to the King’s royal decree, Somu must remove **only the well itself**, and not a single grain of the surrounding imperial river sand!
Therefore, Master Lingaiah, step forward with your measuring tools, hold back all the river sand, and separate the water-hole from the surrounding earth, so we can lift the hole into our carts!'

Lingaiah stared in utter bewilderment:
'Separate the hole from the sand? Art thou insane, Tenali? A well is an empty space inside the ground! How can anyone hold back the sand and lift empty space into a cart?'

Tenali Raman smiled with devastating logic:
'Precisely, Master Lingaiah!
A well is simply the space where water gathers. It removes nothing from the river, and when the monsoon rains arrive, the river will fill it and flow over it harmlessly!
Thou didst demand an impossible decree merely out of jealous spite to ruin an honest neighbor who waters vegetables for the city!'

King Krishnadevaraya saw through Lingaiah’s petty malice.
The King revoked the order, permitted Somu to use the water freely, and fined Lingaiah fifty silver coins for filing frivolous and vindictive lawsuits.
Somu’s gourds flourished, and Tenali’s wit once again shielded the humble from bureaucratic cruelty.
moral: Demands born of arbitrary malice are defeated by claiming the natural boundaries that define them.
